Series::maximum¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::maximum(const Series& rhs) const -> Series
Series::maximum(double rhs) const -> Series

What It Does¶

Returns the elementwise maximum between self and rhs.

This is a comparison operator, not a reduction. It does not ask “what is the largest value in this tensor?” It asks “at each position, which side wins?”

That distinction matters because maximum() participates in broadcasting and in autograd. A scalar overload behaves like “compare every element against one threshold-like value,” while the Series overload behaves like “compare two shapes under ordinary broadcasting rules.”

Parameters¶

rhs (const Series& or double)

The other operand.

For maximum(const Series& rhs):

  • rhs is broadcast against self

  • the result dtype is the promoted dtype of the two operands

  • both operands remain ordinary values; neither side is treated specially as a “bound”

For maximum(double rhs):

  • every element of self is compared against the same scalar

  • the scalar is materialized onto self’s lane, so the result stays on self’s dtype/platform path rather than becoming a separate broadcasted tensor value in a wider promoted dtype

Returns¶

Series A new series containing the winner at each broadcasted position.

Gradient¶

maximum() is differentiable in both operands.

The backward rule is:

  • gradient flows to self where self >= rhs

  • gradient flows to rhs where self < rhs

The important edge case is the tie.

Note

Tie-breaking convention When self[i] == rhs[i], the full gradient goes to self, not split across both operands and not mirrored to rhs. This matches the inclusive-boundary rule used by clamp_min and clamp_max, so the comparison family behaves consistently at boundaries.

Examples¶

Example 1. The Series overload broadcasts a row-shaped peer across the leading dimension.

auto grid = pluss::make_series(
    std::vector<double>{1, 5, 3, 4, 2, 8},
    {2, 3});
auto peer = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{2, 6, 1}, {3});

std::cout << grid.maximum(peer);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[2, 6, 3],
  [4, 6, 8]]

Each row of grid is compared against the same [2, 6, 1] peer. This is often the most readable form when you want a per-column floor without calling it a clamp.

Example 2. The scalar overload compares every element against one shared value.

std::cout << grid.maximum(4.5);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[4.5, 5, 4.5],
  [4.5, 4.5, 8]]

Only positions below 4.5 are raised. Positions already above the scalar pass through unchanged.

Example 3. At a tie, the output is shared but the gradient is not: the tied position attributes its derivative to self.

auto a = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{1, 5, 2}, {3});
auto b = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{4, 2, 2}, {3});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = a.maximum(b);
y.sum().reverse();
std::cout << "y=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "da=" << a.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "db=" << b.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 5, 2]
da=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 1]
db=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0, 0]

Index 2 is the interesting one: both operands are 2, so both values determine the output numerically, but only a receives the derivative there.

Notes¶

  • maximum() is non-mutating. The in-place sibling maximum_() exists, but this page documents the value-returning surface.

  • maximum(x, scalar) is often the clearer spelling when the scalar is acting as a conceptual lower floor; clamp_min is the clearer spelling when you want to emphasize the one-sided-bound intent.

  • This is not amax. If you want a reduction over an axis, use the reduction surface instead.

See Also¶

  • Series::minimum: the elementwise counterpart. Ties still favor self there as well.

  • Series::clamp_min: one-sided lower bound with the same inclusive boundary behavior.

  • Series::clamp_max: one-sided upper bound built from the same comparison family.
